summary: In the case of Cyprus v. Turkey, the Republic of Cyprus brought an inter-State application against Turkey, raising, among other issues, the treatment of the Roma and Traveller community—referred to in the judgment as the “Gypsy community”—in northern Cyprus. The case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma and Travellers, who faced discrimination, restrictions on movement, and denial of access to education and property rights in the territory under Turkish control. Following the Turkish military intervention in northern Cyprus in 1974, Roma and Traveller families living in the area experienced severe hardship: they were prevented from returning to their homes, faced obstacles in accessing their property, and were subjected to social exclusion and inadequate living conditions. The European Court of Human Rights examined a wide range of Convention rights, including Articles 3 (prohibition of degrading treatment), 5 (liberty and security), 8 (respect for private and family life), 9 (freedom of religion), 10 (freedom of expression), 13 (effective remedy), and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education). The Court found multiple violations, notably of Articles 3, 8, 9, 10, 13, and Protocol No. 1, confirming that the Roma and Traveller community had suffered from degrading treatment, denial of home and property rights, and lack of effective remedies. This landmark judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights, as it recognised the compounded discrimination faced by these communities in conflict zones, reflecting a broader historical pattern of marginalisation across Europe.
